\]
so
\[
n=-12q.
\]
Also,
\[
x^2y^2+x^2z^2+y^2z^2=(xy+xz+yz)^2-2xyz(x+y+z)=q^2,
\]
so
\[
q^2=n-11.
\]
Thus
\[
q^2+11=-12q \implies q^2+12q+11=0 \implies (q+1)(q+11)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
q=-1 \quad\text{or}\quad q=-11,
\]
giving
\[
n=12 \quad\text{or}\quad n=132.
\]
So the greatest possible \(n\) is at most \(132\).

Now check \(n=132\). The polynomial becomes
\[
x^3-22x^2+121x-400=(x-16)(x^2-6x+25),
\]
whose roots are
\[
16,\quad 3+4i,\quad 3-4i.
\]
Choose
\[
\alpha=4,\qquad \beta=-2+i,\qquad \gamma=-2-i.
\]
Then
\[
\alpha^2=16,\quad \beta^2=3-4i,\quad \gamma^2=3+4i,
\]
so these squares are exactly the roots. Also
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=4+(-2+i)+(-2-i)=0.
\]
The possible sums come from independently choosing signs of \(4\), \(-2+i\), and \(-2-i\), giving
\[
0,\quad \pm 8,\quad \pm(4-2i),\quad \pm(4+2i),
\]
which are exactly \(7\) distinct values.

Therefore the greatest possible integer is
\[
\boxed{132}.
\]
